title: How things work
description: Use everyday motion to see how air and machines work.
author: claude

topic.title: How things work
topic.description: Use everyday motion to see how air and machines work.

concepts.title: Lift
concepts.hook: A paper glider has no engine, yet its wing can hold it up while air moves past. When it slows, that upward force fades.
concepts.rule: A wing makes lift when air flows past it and is turned down. The air pushes the wing up. Lift must match weight for steady level flight.

claims.text: Lift needs motion between a wing and air.
A wing turns air and gets an upward force; in steady level flight lift balances weight.

items.stem: A student throws a paper plane across a classroom. As it slows, what may happen to lift?

options.text: It can weaken.
options.feedback: Less relative airflow can reduce the wing's upward force, so the glider may sink.

options.text: It must grow with no air flow.
options.feedback: The wing needs air moving past it to make the force that holds it up.

items.stem: On a train, a student holds a small paper wing outside a moving air stream, then in it. When can it feel a push?

options.text: When air flows past it.
options.feedback: The force comes from the wing changing the path of moving air, which pushes back.

options.text: Only when all nearby air is still.
options.feedback: Still air relative to the wing offers no steady stream to turn downward.

items.stem: A toy glider weighs 2 newtons. For steady level flight, about how much upward lift must balance that weight?

options.text: 2 newtons.
options.feedback: In level flight at steady height, upward and downward forces match rather than add.

options.text: 4 newtons.
options.feedback: Twice the weight would leave an upward imbalance instead of steady level flight.

items.stem: A wing sends air downward. Which other force fits Newton's third law?

options.text: Air pushes the wing upward.
options.feedback: Turning air down and receiving an upward push are two sides of the interaction.

options.text: Air pushes the wing only backward.
options.feedback: Drag can act backward, but the downward turn also has an upward force pair.

items.stem: A glider slows in still air, yet its mass stays the same. Why may it start to descend?

options.text: Less airflow can mean less lift.
options.feedback: A slower wing may turn less air downward each second, so lift can fall below weight.

options.text: Slower air raises lift because it stays near the wing longer.
options.feedback: Time near the wing alone does not replace enough flow to balance weight.

items.stem: For a paper plane cruising level, lift points up while weight points ___.

options.text: Down.
options.feedback: Those opposite forces balance if its height and speed are steady in this simple picture.

options.text: Forward.
options.feedback: The plane flies forward. Its weight still pulls down toward the ground.

items.stem: A model wing lifts in a wind tunnel. A student expects the same lift when it moves just as fast in a vacuum. What is the flaw?

options.text: The wing has no air to turn down.
options.feedback: Matching speed is not enough: the wing needs air to receive an upward push.

options.text: Matching speed guarantees matching lift, whatever surrounds the wing.
options.feedback: The surrounding air is part of the force interaction, so removing it changes the result.

items.stem: Put the two links of wing lift in order.

options.text: First: the wing turns moving air down.
options.feedback: The altered air flow is the action that leads to the force on the wing.

options.text: Next: the air pushes the wing up.
options.feedback: That reaction helps support the craft and must match weight in level flight.

misconceptions.name: Shape alone lifts
misconceptions.correction: A still wing needs moving air to make lift.

misconceptions.name: Air is not pushed
misconceptions.correction: Wings turn air; the air pushes back on them.

quest.title: Try a paper wing
quest.detail: Fold a paper glider. Watch what happens as it slows. Mark the air flow and the lift path on a sketch.

concepts.title: How a multirotor turns
concepts.hook: A quadcopter can yaw in place while its four rotors stay horizontal; it changes the balance of their turning forces.
concepts.rule: A multirotor changes motor speeds to shift thrust. Uneven thrust tilts it in pitch or roll; a change in the spin force balance turns it in yaw.

claims.text: A gap in motor speeds can make a drone pitch or roll.
Yaw comes from a change in the balance of rotor turning force.

items.stem: At a school drone demo, one side's rotors push harder. Which motion may begin?

options.text: A tilt toward the weaker side.
options.feedback: Unequal upward push makes a turning effect on the craft before it moves sideways.

options.text: Perfectly level flight with no change.
options.feedback: A left-right thrust gap cannot leave the force balance exactly as it was.

items.stem: In a college lab, a four-rotor craft turns its nose while hovering. What changed?

options.text: The balance of rotor spin effects.
options.feedback: Yaw comes from uneven turning moments, even while total upward thrust can still hold height.

options.text: Its GPS invented a steering wheel.
options.feedback: Position data can guide control, but the physical turn comes from rotor forces.

items.stem: A drone hovers on four rotors at 2 newtons each. To pitch nose down while total thrust stays at 8 newtons, each rear rotor rises to 2.5. What thrust must each front rotor give?

options.text: 1.5 newtons.
options.feedback: The stronger rear pair gives five newtons. The front pair must share three to keep total thrust at eight.

options.text: 2.5 newtons.
options.feedback: Equal front and rear thrust would not create the pitch change in this toy setup.

items.stem: A drone pitches nose down. Which simple cause fits?

options.text: Rear thrust exceeds front thrust.
options.feedback: The rear side lifts more, rotating the body toward a lower nose.

options.text: All rotors push equally at all times.
options.feedback: Equal front and rear forces do not create the needed pitch moment in this setup.

items.stem: A quadcopter hovers with equal rotor thrust. Why are opposite spin directions still needed?

options.text: They can cancel yaw turning effects.
options.feedback: Even when each rotor lifts equally, its spin can turn the craft. Opposite spins help balance that turn.

options.text: Equal thrust alone cancels every turning effect.
options.feedback: Equal thrust balances upward force, but rotor spin can still twist the craft around its vertical axis.

items.stem: Rolling changes the craft's tilt from side to side; yaw turns it around the ___ axis.

options.text: Vertical.
options.feedback: A nose turn in place is yaw, which differs from a side tilt or forward pitch.

options.text: Front-to-back.
options.feedback: Rotation around that axis describes roll, not the nose turning left or right.

items.stem: GPS reports that a drone drifted left, and its controller speeds up rotors. A student says GPS itself pushed it right. What is the flaw?

options.text: The motors made the correcting force.
options.feedback: GPS supplied a position clue; the controller used it to change rotor forces that moved the craft.

options.text: The position signal is the force that moves the craft.
options.feedback: Information about a drift can guide motion, but a radio signal does not provide the needed thrust.

items.stem: Match the two drone motions with their force patterns.

options.text: Roll
options.feedback: A lateral imbalance tips the craft around its front-to-back axis.

options.text: Unequal side-to-side thrust
options.feedback: A stronger push on one side can tip the craft about its front-to-back axis.

options.text: Yaw
options.feedback: The nose turns left or right while the body spins about its upright axis.

options.text: Unequal rotor spin moments
options.feedback: The spin forces no longer cancel, so they can twist the craft in place.

misconceptions.name: GPS steers motors
misconceptions.correction: GPS can aid position, but speed changes at motors make the turn.

misconceptions.name: All speeds same for turn
misconceptions.correction: A turn needs a change in the balance of motor forces.

sources.title: Mathematical Modeling of Quadcopter Dynamics
sources.publisher: Qikai Huang, Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology

sources.title: VNAV Lab 3: Modelling and control of UAVs

quest.title: Sketch four motors
quest.detail: Draw a top view of a four-motor craft. Mark which side needs more thrust for a roll. Label yaw, pitch, and roll.

concepts.title: Batteries and flight time
concepts.hook: Doubling a drone battery's energy need not double flight time: its extra mass also makes the motors work harder.
concepts.rule: Flight time rests on usable battery energy and how fast the motors spend it. A larger battery adds energy and weight, so time need not rise in step with size.

claims.text: Flight time depends on stored energy and the rate at which it is used.
A heavy battery adds weight, so the craft needs more lift.

items.stem: A school drone carries a heavier battery with more energy. What happens to flight time?

options.text: It may rise by less than energy did.
options.feedback: The extra mass raises the force and power needed to stay aloft.

options.text: It must double exactly.
options.feedback: That assumes the motors use energy at the old rate despite the added weight.

items.stem: At a hostel robotics meet, a craft carries a heavy camera. What likely changes in hover?

options.text: The motors need more lift.
options.feedback: The extra load adds weight, so the rotors must supply more upward force.

options.text: The battery stops using energy.
options.feedback: Higher load does not remove the power cost of spinning the rotors.

items.stem: A drone uses a 120 watt-hour battery at 60 watts in hover. A heavier 180 watt-hour battery raises hover power to 90 watts. About how long can it fly in this ideal model?

options.text: 2 hours.
options.feedback: The larger battery stores more energy, but its added weight makes the motors use power faster.

options.text: 3 hours.
options.feedback: Dividing the new energy by the old power ignores the extra load in this toy flight.

items.stem: Two batteries store equal energy but one is heavier. In the same craft, which may give shorter flight?

options.text: The heavier battery.
options.feedback: It asks the motors to support more mass while providing no extra stored energy.

options.text: The lighter battery must always use more power.
options.feedback: With all else equal, extra mass tends to raise rather than lower hover demand.

items.stem: A larger battery stores more energy, yet a drone gains little flight time. Why can both observations be true?

options.text: Added battery mass can raise hover power.
options.feedback: Extra energy helps, but the motors may spend it faster while lifting the heavier craft.

options.text: Energy and flight time must rise in the same ratio.
options.feedback: That ratio holds only if power use stays the same, which added mass can change.

items.stem: To guess flight time, divide stored energy by how fast the drone uses it. What is that rate?

options.text: Power use.
options.feedback: A craft that spends energy faster drains the same store in less time.

options.text: Rotor count alone.
options.feedback: The number of rotors does not state how fast all of them use energy.

items.stem: A heavier battery stores twice the energy, and a student predicts exactly twice the flight time. Which missing factor could break that prediction?

options.text: The added weight can raise power use.
options.feedback: The larger energy store can drain faster because the rotors must carry more mass.

options.text: Battery energy alone fixes flight time.
options.feedback: Flight time depends on both usable energy and the rate at which the motors use it.

items.stem: Which line best explains why flight-time charts are estimates?

options.text: Useable energy and power draw can both change.
options.feedback: Wind, payload, and battery mass affect how fast the stored energy is spent.

options.text: Minutes depend only on battery colour.
options.feedback: Paint tells us no useful fact about how much charge the cell holds or uses.

misconceptions.name: Double size, double time
misconceptions.correction: More battery adds weight, so time need not scale with size.

misconceptions.name: Weight costs nothing
misconceptions.correction: More weight needs more lift and motor work.

sources.title: Flying Batteries: In-flight Battery Switching to Increase Multirotor Flight Time
sources.publisher: Jain and Mueller, University of California Berkeley

quest.title: Draw an energy trade
quest.detail: Sketch two made-up batteries. Add arrows for more stored energy and more mass. Say how each may change flight time.

concepts.title: Flight sensors
concepts.hook: A roof can block a drone's map signal. Yet the drone still feels a quick tilt.
concepts.rule: An IMU senses quick motion and turning. GPS helps locate the craft when signals are clear. A barometer reads air pressure to help track height. Each clue can be imperfect.

claims.text: An IMU can sense a fast turn and a change in speed.
GPS can help find a place. A barometer reads air pressure to help track height.

items.stem: At a school lab, a drone tilts quickly under an awning. Which sensor can notice that motion?

options.text: The inertial sensor.
options.feedback: The IMU feels a quick spin or push. It needs no clear view of the sky.

options.text: Only the satellite receiver.
options.feedback: Satellites help place the drone on a map. A local sensor feels its fast tilt.

items.stem: On a train platform under a roof, a drone's map dot wanders. What may have weakened?

options.text: The satellite position clue.
options.feedback: A roof can block or bounce the signal. The map dot may drift, though tilt sensing works.

options.text: The idea that air has pressure.
options.feedback: A shaky map dot is about position signals, not proof that air pressure vanished.

items.stem: Under a roof, GPS reports 18 metres of height but its signal is poor. A calibrated barometer reports 12 metres. If the weak GPS reading is ignored, what height estimate remains?

options.text: 12 metres.
options.feedback: The calibrated pressure clue remains when the poor satellite reading is set aside in this toy case.

options.text: 18 metres.
options.feedback: That repeats the GPS reading even though the premise says its signal is poor under the roof.

items.stem: Which sensor mainly gives a pressure clue used for height?

options.text: A barometer.
options.feedback: Air pressure changes with height, though weather and other effects make it an imperfect clue.

options.text: A GPS antenna alone.
options.feedback: GPS times signals from space. It does not feel the air around the craft.

items.stem: A drone briefly loses GPS under a roof but keeps moving. Why can its controller still use IMU data?

options.text: The IMU senses quick motion between location clues.
options.feedback: The IMU tracks quick turns and moves while the GPS signal is weak. Its errors can grow.

options.text: The IMU gives exact map coordinates without satellites.
options.feedback: The IMU senses motion. It cannot tell an exact map spot by itself.

items.stem: A quick spin is sensed by an IMU; a map location can be aided by ___.

options.text: Satellite signals.
options.feedback: GPS uses several space signals to find a place. The tilt sensor works on board.

options.text: A fan blade.
options.feedback: A blade moves air but cannot supply the remote timing data used for position.

items.stem: A GPS dot wanders under a roof. A student averages its readings and calls the result exact. What remains uncertain?

options.text: Blocked signals can keep the location wrong.
options.feedback: A roof can block or bend signals. Taking their average may still leave the dot wrong.

options.text: Averaging always removes every roof-related error.
options.feedback: Repeated readings can share the same source of error, so their mean need not be exact.

items.stem: Which explanation fits a drone under a school roof?

options.text: Tilt sensing may work while GPS gets worse.
options.feedback: The IMU feels movement on board. A roof may block the space signals.

options.text: All sensors fail at the same time.
options.feedback: The roof may hurt one clue while the on-board tilt sensor still works.

misconceptions.name: GPS senses all turns
misconceptions.correction: The IMU gives quick turn and motion clues.

misconceptions.name: One sensor is perfect
misconceptions.correction: Signals and readings can have limits, so each clue can err.

quest.title: Make a sensor map
quest.detail: On paper, draw a drone and link tilt, place, and height to IMU, GPS, and barometer. Add one limit for each.

concepts.title: Why birds flap but planes do not
concepts.hook: A bird can flap for both lift and forward push; a jet keeps fixed wings while its engine supplies the forward push.
concepts.rule: Bird flaps can help give lift and forward push. A plane’s fixed wings make lift as air moves past them, while an engine or propeller gives forward push.

claims.text: Bird wing flaps can provide lift and thrust.
A plane can use fixed wings for lift and engines or propellers for thrust.

items.stem: A student sees a bird flap beside a train. What can the wing stroke help provide?

options.text: Lift and forward push.
options.feedback: The changing wing motion can push air in ways that support and propel the bird.

options.text: Only a way to make noise.
options.feedback: The moving wing interacts with air to create forces that matter for flight.

items.stem: During a school trip, a jet passes overhead with wings that do not flap. Why can it stay up?

options.text: Air flows past its fixed wings.
options.feedback: The engine gives forward motion, and the moving air lets the wings make lift.

options.text: Its wings are secretly flapping.
options.feedback: Fixed wings can support flight without the wingbeats used by many birds.

items.stem: A plane weighs 500 newtons in steady level flight. Its engine gives 200 newtons of forward thrust. About how much upward lift must its fixed wings still make?

options.text: 500 newtons.
options.feedback: The wings balance weight vertically. Engine thrust acts forward and does not replace that lift.

options.text: 200 newtons.
options.feedback: That is the forward engine thrust. The upward wing force must balance the plane’s weight.

items.stem: On a plane, which part mainly gives forward thrust?

options.text: The engine or propeller.
options.feedback: It pushes the craft forward so air can flow over the fixed wings.

options.text: The painted wing stripe.
options.feedback: Paint can mark a wing but does not supply the forward force for flight.

items.stem: A bird glides without flapping and a plane flies with fixed wings. What common condition lets both wings lift?

options.text: Air must flow past and be turned down.
options.feedback: Either wing can receive an upward push when it deflects moving air.

options.text: Both wings must flap to keep air moving.
options.feedback: Gliding birds and fixed plane wings can meet moving air without a flap.

items.stem: A jet engine mainly gives thrust; the fixed wings mainly give ___.

options.text: Lift.
options.feedback: Keeping these roles apart helps explain flight without making the wing flap.

options.text: The engine's main forward thrust.
options.feedback: A jet engine provides the main thrust; moving air over fixed wings provides lift.

items.stem: A plane’s engine stops, yet it glides for a while. A student says only flapping wings can lift without engine thrust. What is missing?

options.text: Forward glide keeps air moving past fixed wings.
options.feedback: The plane can trade height for motion, and its fixed wings can still make lift.

options.text: Engine thrust is the only possible source of wing airflow.
options.feedback: Airflow can persist during a glide even when the engine no longer pushes forward.

items.stem: Which comparison captures the shared rule?

options.text: Both use air to make lift, by different motions.
options.feedback: Bird wingbeats can add thrust, while a plane engine drives air past its fixed wings.

options.text: Both use engines to flap wings.
options.feedback: Birds use muscles, and most planes do not flap their fixed wings.

misconceptions.name: All wings must flap
misconceptions.correction: A fixed wing can lift when air moves past it.

misconceptions.name: Engine makes all lift
misconceptions.correction: The engine gives forward thrust; the wing makes most lift.

sources.title: Birds Repurpose the Role of Drag and Lift to Take Off and Land

quest.title: Spot two pushes
quest.detail: Watch a bird and a plane clip. Draw an arrow for forward push and one for lift on each.

concepts.title: How a ceiling fan moves air
concepts.hook: A fan can cool sweaty skin in a warm classroom, yet the air stays warm. Where did the cooling happen?
concepts.rule: Angled fan blades push air and make it flow through the room. The breeze can help people feel cooler, but the fan does not make cold air.

claims.text: A ceiling fan moves room air with rotating blades.
A breeze can aid cooling at the skin, but a fan does not make cold air.

items.stem: A classroom fan starts while the window stays shut. What reaches a student's face?

options.text: Faster moving room air.
options.feedback: The blades push air through the room, giving a breeze without making new cold air.

options.text: Air made cold inside the motor.
options.feedback: A ceiling fan has no cooling coil; the sensation comes from moving air.

items.stem: During monsoon heat, a hostel fan runs in an empty room. Who feels its breeze?

options.text: No person in that room.
options.feedback: The motor still moves air, but the main cooling effect needs a person beneath it.

options.text: The walls feel the same chill as skin.
options.feedback: A breeze helps a person lose heat; walls do not sweat or sense a breeze.

items.stem: A ceiling fan makes a breeze in an empty room. If only the breeze changes, about how many degrees Celsius does it lower the room air temperature?

options.text: 0 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: Air motion can cool skin through evaporation, but the breeze alone does not remove heat from room air.

options.text: 3 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: A cooler feeling needs a person in the breeze. Moving air alone does not chill the room.

items.stem: Why can the same air feel cooler when it moves over skin?

options.text: It helps sweat evaporate.
options.feedback: Moving air helps sweat dry. That can cool skin while the room air stays warm.

options.text: The fan makes ice in the air.
options.feedback: The blades move air; they do not use a cooling cycle to freeze moisture.

items.stem: A tilted fan blade spins and makes a breeze. Why does the tilt matter?

options.text: It redirects nearby air as it turns.
options.feedback: The blade pushes air along; that moving air can then pass over skin.

options.text: A blade cools the air mainly by touching it.
options.feedback: Contact and spin alone do not remove heat; the tilt helps move the air.

items.stem: A fan moves room air; an air conditioner can lower the air's ___.

options.text: Temperature.
options.feedback: The devices can feel similar to a person, but only one removes heat from the room air.

options.text: Number of blades.
options.feedback: Blade count describes a fan, not the heat content of room air.

items.stem: A fan runs for an hour in an empty classroom. A student expects the room to be cooler when people return. What did the student mix up?

options.text: Skin cooling and room air cooling.
options.feedback: The breeze can help a person lose heat, but an empty room has no skin to cool.

options.text: Air movement slowly turns warm air into cold air.
options.feedback: The fan moves the same air; it does not run a heat-removing cooling cycle.

items.stem: Which line best explains a fan during a hot exam?

options.text: Moving air can cool people without chilling the room.
options.feedback: The breeze raises evaporation and heat loss at skin while air temperature may stay near the same.

options.text: The motor removes all room heat.
options.feedback: A spinning motor uses energy and is not a device that carries heat outdoors.

misconceptions.name: Fan makes cold air
misconceptions.correction: A fan moves the air already in the room.

sources.title: Energy-Saving Hacks To Beat the Summer Heat

quest.title: Map a breeze
quest.detail: With the fan on, hold a light ribbon safely away from the blades. Sketch which way the air flows.
